column1: # Published manuscript scans Milah offers for transcription.
# One row per manuscript, tab-separated. Only `url` is required: everything else
# is read from the holding library's own record. Blank lines and lines opening
# with # are ignored, so a manuscript can be annotated with why it is here.
# url    the address as copied from the library's viewer
# title  overrides the library's own title, which sometimes names a whole codex
#        where only a part of it is being transcribed
# book   the OSIS book code, where the scan is of one book; only used to group
#        the list, and empty for a codex covering many
# width  pixels wide to request, default 1024. Honoured only where the library
#        lets a size be asked for: Cambridge serves any width but caps delivery
#        at 2000, while OPenn publishes fixed derivatives and chooses for you.
# folios the part of a codex this row offers, as two of the labels the library
#        itself uses, written 1r..21v. Endpoints are found by position in the
#        page list, never by arithmetic on the folio number: Cambridge's first
#        image is the front cover, so 1r is image 3 in this codex and image
#        something else in the next. Written with .. rather than a hyphen,
#        because OPenn labels endleaves i-r, where the hyphen is part of the
#        label. Empty is the whole codex, which is what every row was before
#        this column existed.
# shelfmark  overrides a record that states none. A bare IIIF manifest carries
#        no shelfmark at all, and it is what tells two manuscripts of the same
#        book apart — and what the picker heads a manuscript's books with.
# licence  the terms, where the library states them somewhere a IIIF manifest
#        has no field for: the Bodleian puts them in its attribution line and
#        leaves `license` unset. Copy what the library says. It is not a place
#        to decide what terms a scan ought to have — a scan whose terms are
#        unclear is one nobody may use, and inventing them does not change that.
# repository  overrides a record that states none — every bare IIIF manifest
#        below leaves "Held at" blank without it.
# status   empty (normal — url is read as above) or `unavailable`. A manuscript
#        known to exist but never photographed, or not currently reachable:
#        Cambridge MS Oo.1.16 has no viewer to copy a link from, and the
#        British Library's own catalogue calls Add MS 26964's images "currently
#        unavailable". `url` may be blank, or may hold a plain catalogue page to
#        learn more from — either way nothing is fetched from it. `title`,
#        `shelfmark`, `repository` and `note` are supplied by hand, since there
#        is no record to read them from.
# note     why an `unavailable` row has nothing to open. Shown to a reader
#        before they can wonder why the entry is greyed out; a row with none
#        prints a warning when this file is regenerated.
# The three below are judgements about the text rather than facts about the
# object, which is why no library record carries them and why they are written
# here by hand. Milah offers them when a scan is opened, so a transcription
# starts out saying what is already known about the manuscript.
# translatedFrom  what the Hebrew renders, where it renders anything:
#        "Translated from the Greek". Empty is not itself an answer — the
#        column beside it is what says whether anything has been settled.
# translationCertainty  how firmly that is held. One of:
#          certain             established
#          uncertain           stated, not settled
#          original            not a translation; an original Hebrew text
#          original-uncertain  probably not a translation
#        Empty means nobody has recorded an answer, which is a different thing
#        from "not a translation", and is what every row here says until it is
#        filled in. Milah marks an unsettled answer with a question mark rather
#        than stating it flat: for several of these manuscripts — Shem Tov's
#        Matthew above all — that is the whole argument.
# exemplar  the older manuscript this one copies, where it is known to copy
#        one: "Copied from Cambridge MS Oo.1.32". Gaster Hebrew MS 1616 is
#        Thomas Yeates's copy of exactly that, which is the case this exists
#        for.
# Rows may name one address as often as they like: the library's record is read
# once per run and each row takes its own slice of it.
# Titles here are the book alone, not "Mark (Cambridge, MS Oo.1.32)": the
# shelfmark is a field of its own and the picker shows it above the books it
# holds, so naming the manuscript again in every title prints it twice.
# Regenerate after editing:  python src/build_scan_manifest.py
url
column7: licence

column1: # Three more from the National Library of Israel's Ktiv project, which
# aggregates other libraries' Hebrew manuscripts as well as its own. Its
# manifests are addressed by an internal document id rather than by
# shelfmark — the "dedupmrg…" below — which is found in the page source of
# the manuscript's own reading-room page (nli.org.il/en/manuscripts/…) and
# is the only key that returns anything: the same endpoint asked with the
# catalogue's system number answers with a valid manifest of zero pages,
# which reads exactly like a manuscript that was never photographed. The
# images host is open to a plain client; www.nli.org.il is not, so a link
# here has to be the manifest and never the reading-room page.
# NLI's own terms, quoted below, come from the pages its manifests link to
# rather than being summarised: two of the three are outright public domain,
# and the third is a depositor's non-commercial restriction.
# Poznanski's working copy, c. 1900: the Even Bohan collated across four
# witnesses at once — Breslau 59 as its base, with the British Museum, Rome
# and Paris copies noted against it. Not a medieval witness but a scholar's
# comparative edition of them, in a clear modern hand, with editorial notes
# in German: "Johannes … Cap. 2" heads one page, a note on Luke of Antioch
# another. It covers more than the Even Bohan's twelfth gate — John begins
# on page 275, Luke on 306, Mark on 401 — but where each ends is not
# recorded anywhere, and that order is not the order anything else in this
# file is in, so the whole volume is offered rather than four ranges guessed
# at.
https://iiif.nli.org.il/IIIFv21/DOCID/dedupmrg1219421241/manifest
column2: Even Bohan, collated with the Gospels (Poznanski's copy)

# Johann Kemper's two manuscripts at Uppsala. Kemper was born Moses ben Aaron
# of Kraków, a Sabbatean who converted in 1696 and taught Hebrew at Uppsala;
# he translated the New Testament from Syriac into Hebrew, which is why his
# Matthew below is titled with the Aramaic name of the Gospel rather than a
# Hebrew one. Uppsala publishes on Alvin, which serves no IIIF and no API at

column1: # Known but with nothing to open — offered anyway, so a transcriber sees these
# exist rather than having to already know to look for them. Each is the best
# remaining Even Bohan witness after the four above; none is guessed at, and
# each note below is what its own library or record states, not an inference.
# Columns from here on: url title book width folios shelfmark licence
# repository status note.
# The best witness of all, and out of copyright: 206 folios, dated 1696, one
# of the four purest texts and Howard's base manuscript for 1:1–23:22. The
# British Library's own catalogue record states its surrogate is "digital
# images currently unavailable" — true as of the 2023 cyberattack, and worth
# rechecking, since a library recovering its infrastructure is not the same as
# a manuscript that was never photographed.
https://searcharchives.bl.uk/catalog/032-003313863
column10: Even Bohan by Shem Ṭov Ibn Shapruṭ, 1696, 206 ff. Digitised and viewable on the British Library's old site as of December 2019 (Wayback Machine snapshot of the viewer link); the Library's own catalogue now records the surrogate as "digital images currently unavailable" since the 2023 cyberattack, and its new IIIF platform (bl.digirati.io) does not yet list it. Worth rechecking as the Library's infrastructure recovers.

https://searcharchives.bl.uk/catalog/040-003376870
column2: James and Jude, dedicated to Henry VIII
column10: Digitised under the Hebrew Manuscripts Digitisation Project, 49 ff., 16th century (Margoliouth no. 164): Shepreve's dedication ff. 1v-23r, James ff. 23r-44r, Jude ff. 44r-49v. The only surrogate the catalogue lists is the Library's own viewer, which it annotates "digital images currently unavailable" — that site has been down since the 2023 cyberattack. Not among the British Library manuscripts OPenn mirrors, and the Library's new IIIF platform publishes no way to find a manuscript by shelfmark.

column1: # Beware also of three unrelated works of the same title, all with manifests:
# Bodleian Opp. Add. 8° 28 and Munich Cod.hebr. 338 are Kalonymos ben

# Cambridge MS Oo.1.16 — the manuscript REV_CochinOo.1.16.2_hebrew_commented.osis
# transcribes, and the second half of the Buchanan acquisition alongside MS
# Oo.1.32, above. It is not on Cambridge Digital Library: searching CUDL for
# "Oo.1.16" returns exactly one result, and that one — MS Add. 4541 — is an

# this manuscript's own binding, not Oo.1.16 itself. Described only in print

column10: Not on Cambridge Digital Library. A CUDL search for "Oo.1.16" finds only MS Add. 4541 — a Greek Matthew fragment from its own binding waste, not the manuscript. Described in print: Reif, Hebrew Manuscripts at Cambridge University Library (1997), no. 917.

column1: # The Russian State Library's Guenzburg collection was digitised on Ktiv
# after a 2017 agreement between Russia and Israel, and Ms. Guenzburg 363
# — a 16th/17th-century Italian miscellany of some twenty unrelated Hebrew
# texts bound as one volume — is one of the manuscripts that reached it: its
# own record, found by searching the shelfmark directly, names "ברית חדשה
# (לקוטים)" — New Testament (excerpts) — as one of those texts, Luke
# 17-24 and John 1-6, ff. 48a-59b, and states "Images: Available". Its
# pages are not this text's own, though: the manifest below returns the
# whole 223-page miscellany, numbered Page 1 to Page 223 with no table of
# contents mapping any of its twenty texts to a page range, so which of the
# 223 are the twelve leaves of ff. 48a-59b is not stated anywhere and is not
# guessed at here — book is left blank rather than tagged Luke, since a
# transcriber choosing Luke from the picker would otherwise open this and
# find nineteen unrelated things first. Offered anyway, unsliced, since a
# human paging through by eye can do what a folios range cannot: the
# reading-room viewer is the second address below, easier to browse than
# the bare manifest — https://www.nli.org.il/en/manuscripts/NNL_ALEPH990001465430205171/NLI
https://iiif.nli.org.il/IIIFv21/DOCID/NNL_ALEPH71228769860005171/manifest/IE70811450
